title: Trump stumps for embattled Texas Senate candidate at raucous rally | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in less than a month Wednesday, attacking Democrats and warning about illegal immigration as he stumped for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president haspublicly insultedin personal terms.

Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasinglyuphill battleto hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas.

Republicans arepouring millionsinto bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facinga closer-than-expected raceagainst Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994.

The president’s appearance in San Antonio was vintage Trump, combining lighthearted moments with vicious attacks on his opponents. He joked about his own thinning hair and falsely attacked Talarico as a vegan – noting his wife had told him recently he had been mispronouncing the word. At least a dozen protesters, who interrupted Trump’s rally on several occasions, were removed from the event.

At one point, Trump appeared to try to clarify incendiary remarks he made earlier this week that drew harsh bipartisan backlash when he seemed to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

Speaking at the rally, Trump made similar comments, this time adding, “We’re not going to let that happen.”

One Texas GOP strategist said the event’s effectiveness will be closely watched in the coming days for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state.

The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November isboosting base turnout.

Butsome Republicans, even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too.

“It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said.

Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles.

The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audioobtained by Axioson Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio.

Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.”

But that followed The New York Times last weekpublishing audioof Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.”

Paxton has been plagued byhis own set of scandals, including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.

Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office earlier Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton.

At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.”

Then there’s his frequentribbingof the state attorney general’s appearance.

“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.”

Trump did not repeat that refrain Wednesday night, calling Paxton a “fantastic man” as the two showcased warm relations on stage.

“I’m very proud of him and I think he’s gonna be an unbelievable senator,” Trump said as he invited Paxton to speak.

Paxton, in turn, expressed gratitude to his guest. “Aren’t you guys glad he came to San Antonio?” he asked an enthusiastic crowd.

The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely.

“But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added.

Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump earlier Wednesday, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his planned appearance on stage with the president.

Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — hisapproval rating is 34%in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates.

And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to aNBC News/Telemundo pollearlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino.

Trump sought to juice turnout among his MAGA base Wednesday evening with a focus on border security and other red meat issues, including the attack on Talarico as a vegan — a claim the Democrat has denied. And there were visible efforts to organize, including information about early voting and mail-in ballots for attendees on screens and in handouts.

But Trump’s visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk.

“Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said.

And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side.

“If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative.

The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive.

The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN haspreviously reported. Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved.

But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map.

“A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised  concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary.

“If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added.

But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points.

That’s led to a debate about how much of this year’s close race is a reflection of the candidate matchup or the national environment and an unpopular president.

“If Paxton was a normal person, he probably would still eke it out. I mean, the state’s still structurally conservative,” said one DC-based GOP operative.

And the stakes of this year’s race could be bigger than just control of the Senate in 2027; it could carry ramifications for 2028 and beyond.

The Texas Republican operative compared a potential Talarico win to a “hole in the dam” that could give Democrats momentum to turn the state blue at the presidential level.

Paxton appears to recognize the stakes.

“If we lose Texas, we lose America,” hesaidin a social media post announcing Wednesday’s rally.

This story has been updated with additional developments.
